summary: At a population density of just 12 people per square mile, Mariposa County is one of the most sparsely populated places in California — spread across nearly 1,500 square miles of Sierra Nevada foothill terrain that climbs from oak-studded grasslands around 2,000 feet to granite peaks above 10,000 feet along its eastern boundary, which happens to be the western entrance to Yosemite National Park. That proximity to Yosemite is the defining economic fact here: tourism and the National Park Service anchor the local job market, supplemented by county government and small-scale ranching, meaning employment options are narrow and most positions orbit a single industry. A median home value of $358,000 against a median household income of $65,378 produces a price-to-income ratio around 5.5 — more manageable than coastal California but still a stretch given that high-paying private-sector employers are essentially absent. The town of Mariposa itself offers a compact historic downtown along Highway 140 with a handful of restaurants, a grocery store, and a courthouse built during the Gold Rush era, but evening activity is quiet and amenities thin out fast beyond that strip. Summers bring warm, dry days averaging in the upper 60s to low 70s with abundant sunshine — roughly 9.4 hours a day year-round — while winters are cool and occasionally snowy at higher elevations. With no hospital trauma center, no big-box retail, and a winding two-lane drive of over an hour to reach Merced for routine errands, the tradeoff is stark: extraordinary natural access in exchange for the kind of infrastructural isolation that shapes every daily decision.
